fixes.before: A grammar has cycles iff there exists nonterminal A such that A =>+ A; eliminate unit and epsilon productions
fixes.after: If $A \Rightarrow^+ A$ and $A \Rightarrow^* w$, then $w$ has two parse trees from A (with and without the cycle inserted), so the grammar is ambiguous; every LL(1) grammar is unambiguous, so a grammar with cycles cannot be LL(1).
fixes.reason: Stored answer only restated the definition of a cycle and named an unrelated transformation; replaced with the required proof outline (cycle ⇒ ambiguity ⇒ not LL(1)).
fixes.source: Standard result (Aho, Sethi, Ullman); proof in solution

fixes.before: L* is closed under concatenation and Kleene star; regularity preserved if L is regular
fixes.after: Certificate for $x \in L^C$ ($|x| = n$): a string $y$ with $|y| = n$, $y \ne x$, plus an NP certificate that $y \in L$. Since L has exactly one string of each length, such a $y$ exists iff $x \notin L$, and checking it takes polynomial time, so $L^C \in$ NP.
fixes.reason: Stored answer talked about L* and closure under concatenation, which does not address the question; replaced with the NP-certificate argument for L^C.
